record.text:
Happy 100th birthday, Winnie-the-Pooh! 

Did you know that Winnie was based on a real Canadian-British bear—and that his full name was WINNIPEG?

images.alt: My great grandmother with Winnipeg the bear at Valcartier Camp Canada circa World War I.
My grandmother's brother with Winnipeg the bear at Valcartier Camp Canada circa World War I. (double exposure)
My grandmother and her brother with Winnipeg the bear at Valcartier Camp Canada circa World War I.
Harry Colebourn, who bought Winnipeg the bear at the Winnipeg train station, with the bear at Valcartier Camp Canada circa World War I.

record.text: a masterclass in alt text

images.alt:
Pen and watercolor 

Cowboys again. This time one of our boys has lost his boots. Standing in a field of long grass the cowboy points towards the ground and shouts back to his colleague, “Lil bone people got muh boots.” This makes no sense to the other cowboy who sits atop his horse away from the action. He responds, “Lil wut?” Sure enough in the foreground we see a squad of little bone people scampering through the grass with the stolen cowboy boots. They’re thrilled. How the bone people got the boots off the cowboy is unclear.

Artist’s note: I tend to draw drawings from the same perspective (straight on) most of the time. This idea came about when I was goofin around trying to draw a character from a lower angle. I like that the story unfolds with the foreground, mid-ground, and background all working together. There’s a draft of this one included in the Spooky Pants book. Coming out next week!
